conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: named per-technician accounts with a second factor and requested, logged elevation, with the extra minutes built into the estimate rather than traded away under deadline - a practice with administrative reach into many clients is a higher-value target than any one of them

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: realistic phishing simulation versus staff dignity
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: use realistic pretexts drawn from the client's actual workflow and never cruelty about pay, jobs or bereavement; report aggregate trends to the owner, coach individuals privately, and decline to supply individual results for disciplinary use, because a program that humiliates people teaches them to hide the mistakes that are the earliest detection a small business has

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: enforcing domain authentication to stop impersonation versus keeping the client's own invoicing mail deliverable
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: enumerate senders, observe through a full business cycle, align every legitimate sender, then enforce; on a delivery failure relax first and fix alignment before re-enforcing

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: hardening speed versus proven recoverability
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: recoverability comes first - move it ahead of any disruptive change or restrict that change to the pilot ring until a witnessed restore exists, because a proven restore is the control that limits every other failure including the ones the project itself causes

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: containing and remediating immediately versus preserving the record that explains what happened
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: contain reversibly while capturing the cheap perishable artifacts inline, and never take an irreversible step before the runbook's capture list when an external party may review the incident; if active harm makes capture impossible, contain and record precisely what was lost and why

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: a sensitive detection queue that catches quiet identity attacks versus a queue the fixed per-seat price can fund
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: suppress only characterized benign-normal with an owner and an expiry, protect the top-severity combinations absolutely, and solve remaining volume by fixing the underlying condition, re-scoping or repricing openly - never by looking less

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: the continuous coverage the market expects versus what a small practice's roster can actually deliver
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: state the coverage window, the out-of-hours automated path and the response definition explicitly, let pre-authorized automated containment carry the hours nobody is watching, and be able to name the person who receives the page at three in the morning and what happens if they do not wake up

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: reassuring a frightened owner versus stating only what the evidence supports
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: use the four-part update structure so uncertainty arrives inside a visible plan, treat we do not know yet plus what is being done as a complete answer, and defer the all-clear until it is verified - a retracted all-clear costs more trust than any amount of admitted uncertainty

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: disclosing the practice's own contribution to an incident versus protecting the account
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: disclose in the update where it becomes known internally, paired with the concrete corrective change, and rebuild the relationship with evidence rather than with silence; client exposure dominates the practice's commercial interest

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: keeping incident work in-house versus escalating to a carrier's panel, a specialist responder or counsel
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: treat the trigger list as non-discretionary, hand over a preserved evidence package, and stay in the supporting role rather than competing with the specialist

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: making a quiet quarter feel worth paying for versus reporting only calibrated evidence
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: build the report from dated operational artifacts with denominators and limits, include misses and undone work, and let a successful drill rather than a dramatized threat count carry the value story

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: giving a client the questionnaire answers they need versus staying inside factual evidence
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: supply dated factual statements tied to artifacts, answer unsupported rows as not in place, refuse signature and compliance opinion, and route the determination to the client's counsel, assessor or carrier - an inaccurate answer to an insurer can cost the client far more than an honest gap

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: drills realistic enough to reveal failures versus a small client's tolerance for disruption
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: climb the drill ladder over time, run disruptive stages in isolated environments or outside trading hours, and treat every discovered failure as the return that justifies the disruption

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: growing the account versus the no-fear rule inside a relationship where trust makes pressure more effective
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: source every offer from an observation, present it after stand-down in the ordinary review in the same neutral language used everywhere else, never withhold a cheap in-scope fix to make a paid tier look necessary, sequence the smallest effective step for a stretched client, and record declines in the register without escalation

conflicts_and_dominance.tradeoff: the practice's own confidence in an artifact versus the deterministic gates and the client's own verification
conflicts_and_dominance.resolution: evidence and the gate decide, not conviction: a count is re-derived from the source system, a control is proven by its artifact, a recovery objective is the number measured in this client's own drill, and anything unsupported is reported as not in place

glossary.definition: the set of controls below which the practice will not sell a managed security service at all - typically a second factor on email and remote access, a tested restore path, managed endpoint protection and patching of internet-facing systems; a delivery precondition present identically in every tier, outside discount authority, with only the scope above it negotiable

the internal table pairing each control with the specific loss events it reduces, the mechanism of reduction - prevents initiation, blocks a step, shortens detection, bounds recovery - what it explicitly does not cover and what it depends on to work; the source that makes a tier defensible and an objection answerable

the monthly cost to the practice of serving one seat or one site at a given tier, built from contracted vendor licence cost, platform minimums spread across the whole book, recurring labor minutes measured from the practice's own ticket records, amortized onboarding labor and allocated tooling and overhead; the only legitimate basis for a price

the countable thing the subscription bills on, defined in writing before signature - most often a person with an identity in the client's directory rather than a device or a site - with the definition resolving shared terminals, multi-device users, seasonal staff and service accounts, or it becomes a recurring monthly argument

the agreed mechanism for reconciling billed units against actual units: a named count date, the source system the count is taken from, the cadence, and how additions and reductions take effect; a true-up that only ever counts upward reads to a client as a trap and becomes a retention problem

the price-change rules written at the sale - a vendor licensing pass-through requiring the vendor's own notice as evidence, and a periodic review tied to a named publicly verifiable index or a stated cap - explained aloud at signature so an increase is the execution of a rule rather than the opening of a negotiation

the signed document naming the client legal entity, the in-scope systems, sites, tenants and domains, the explicitly out-of-scope and third-party-owned assets, the permitted actions, the named contacts and out-of-hours approvers and the effective dates, signed by a person with actual authority over each named system; it precedes every technical action

the delivery-phase form of the authorization: the entity, in-scope sites and tenants, the defensive-only clause, the maintenance windows, who may approve a disruptive change, and which third-party-owned assets are carved out

the per-control split of duties between the practice, the client and any third party, agreed at the sale, naming the client duties that are conditions of the service - keeping the staff and device list current, enforcing the second factor including on the owner, approving maintenance windows, reporting suspicions promptly, funding replacement of unsupportable equipment

explaining in plain operational language how businesses of this shape actually get hurt - a reused password harvested by phishing, an invoice altered mid-thread, an unpatched remote-access appliance, a hijacked bookkeeping session - what each mechanism needs to succeed and which control interrupts it; the sanctioned alternative to scare tactics
the compliance test for the no-fear doctrine: if the buyer's decision would be different once they calm down and re-read the proposal, the sale was made on fear and must be unwound rather than banked

the concrete rules for selling to a buyer who cannot evaluate an offer freely - stabilize first and sell later, contract and invoice emergency work separately, a plain-language summary page, a stated cooling-off window before any long commitment, the recovery technician kept out of the upsell conversation, a second pair of eyes on the deal, and a required restatement of tier, price basis, term and one non-coverage

the initial fixed-scope engagement that installs and configures the stack and closes the baseline gaps, priced separately from the subscription, scoped from counted assets, and carrying its own assumptions, change mechanism and acceptance criteria; never given away to win the recurring deal

the named category of duty a client or an incident appears to sit under - sector data-handling duties, payment-card contractual requirements, personal-data protection and breach-notification duties, a customer-imposed or franchisor contractual security schedule, an insurer's prompt-reporting condition, lender or grant conditions - used instead of asserting a specific rule, because the specifics vary by jurisdiction, sector, carrier and contract, change over time, and must be verified currently by the client's own counsel, assessor or carrier

the defined end state of each control at a client - which assets or accounts carry it, what the setting must be, and what artifact proves it - written once as the practice's standard and instantiated per client with its deviations recorded
the reconciled count of in-scope assets or accounts against which every coverage claim is measured; a control is never reported as complete against the number of machines the tool happens to see

a group of machines that receives updates at a defined point in the schedule - pilot machines first, then the general fleet, then production-sensitive systems - so a bad update is discovered on a few tolerant machines rather than everywhere at once

the dated list of systems, accounts or applications that cannot meet the baseline, each carrying the verified constraint, the compensating control, the residual risk in plain language, a named client acceptance and a review date; an exception that is not written down is an undisclosed hole in a baseline the client believes is complete

a different control applied because the baseline one cannot be, chosen to reduce the same exposure by another route - network isolation and removal of mail and web access on a machine that cannot be patched, for example - and recorded alongside the exception it answers, with the isolation tested from the machine rather than assumed

a rarely used administrative account, excluded from routine sign-in policies and kept with its credential offline, that exists so a second-factor or access-policy failure cannot lock the provider and the client out of their own environment; its use raises an alert

a backup copy that cannot be reached or deleted using credentials that exist in the client's production environment, typically held offsite or in a provider-managed tenant and protected by retention locking or immutability where the product supports it

backup storage whose copies cannot be altered or deleted by an administrator credential for a defined window - the property that keeps a backup usable after an attacker obtains administrative access; whether a given client's plan actually provides it, and for how long, is a per-plan fact to be verified rather than assumed

glossary.term: recovery point and recovery time targets
glossary.definition: the client-agreed answers to how much recent work the business can afford to lose and how long it can be down, set in business terms and used as the design constraint and the measurement for restore tests; targets to design against, never guarantees of outcome

recovery time and recovery point expressed as numbers observed in this client's own rehearsed restore - what came back, how far back, how long until it was usable, on what date - rather than as figures asserted in a proposal; an unmeasured objective is an assumption, not a commitment

published records that let receiving mail systems check whether a message claiming to come from the client's domain was sent by a source the domain authorizes; rolled out by enumerating legitimate senders, observing in a monitoring posture through a full business cycle, aligning senders, and only then enforcing

the practice's own security applied to the administrative reach it holds into many client environments - named per-technician accounts, a second factor on every console, secrets in a managed store, requested and logged elevation, prompt offboarding, and a client-visible record of who at the provider can reach what

the standing document that governs the live estate for as long as the subscription runs: the systems, tenants and sites in scope for telemetry and response, the explicit exclusions, the containment actions pre-authorized for immediate use, the actions that always require a named human's approval, and the verified reachable approvers

the operational statement of what monitoring actually is - the hours a human genuinely looks at the queue, what happens to a high-severity alert outside them, and which of acknowledged, triage started, containment attempted or resolved the response target means - derived from the practice's own on-call reality rather than a competitor's brochure

the live answer to what is actually being watched: every asset class paired with a named telemetry source or an explicitly accepted blind-spot entry with a reason and a date, reconciled on cadence to catch dead agents, unmanaged devices, stale accounts and new sites

the repeated unit of work in which a signal from an endpoint, identity, email or backup tool is enriched, judged and dispositioned - closed as benign with a written reason, watched, acted on inside pre-authorization, or escalated into a declared incident - within the coverage window the subscription actually funds

a documented tuning exception that stops a specific benign-normal pattern from raising an alert for one tenant, recording the pattern, the business reason, the approver and an expiry date; an undocumented or perpetual suppression is a disabled detection rather than tuning, and no suppression may cover a declaration-criteria signal

the margin mechanism of the recurring service: total technician minutes attributable to a tenant in a period, taken from the practice's own ticket timestamps and divided by that tenant's billed seats, compared against the labor budget implied by the practice's own price and target margin

the state entered when observable criteria are met and a technician formally declares, switching the engagement from queue work to runbook work: an incident lead is named, the update rhythm starts, evidence preservation begins and action logging becomes mandatory until a lead stands it down in writing

a containment action that stops attacker access while leaving the environment recoverable and the evidence intact - disabling an account, revoking sessions and tokens, blocking a sender, isolating an endpoint while keeping the management channel - as opposed to irreversible remediation such as wiping, reimaging or restoring over live data

the small-business incident class in which an attacker gains use of a mailbox or cloud identity rather than deploying malware, then reads, hides and redirects mail through inbox rules, forwarding and altered payment instructions - which is why identity and mail-flow signals outrank file-level alerts in the triage model

the interval between an attacker first obtaining access and the practice detecting it; it matters commercially as well as technically because log retention windows on small-business cloud plans are often shorter than the dwell time, so the evidence needed to reconstruct the intrusion can expire before anyone looks for it

an incident channel deliberately outside the systems under investigation - a phone call, a text message, a chat account on unrelated infrastructure - used because an attacker holding a mailbox can read the incident thread, delete warnings and impersonate either party in it

the current client-facing statement of what comes back, how far back and what does not come back at all, kept live because the gap between what an owner believes is backed up and what is actually protected - short native cloud retention, an uncovered line-of-business database, a workstation holding the only copy - is where most of the real damage lives

the per-control set of dated artifacts with explicit pass or fail that closes the hardening project and later feeds the recurring report and any control mapping; a control without its artifact against its stated population is reported as not delivered

the living list of exposures that remain open because the client declined, deferred or cannot yet fund the fix, each naming the exposure, the recommendation, the decision, the decision-maker, the date, any compensating control and a review date, presented at every review with the presentation recorded

the line at which control mapping stops: the practice supplies dated factual statements pointing at artifacts and answers unsupported rows as not in place, and does not certify, audit, assess, attest, sign the client's questionnaire, answer in the client's name, or opine on whether the client is compliant

competency_questions_covered: What security work is this practice allowed to sell and perform at all, and what must be signed before anyone touches a prospect's systems?
How do we create demand through understanding rather than fear, and how is an objection like 'we are too small to be a target' answered?
What may we honestly promise about what the package does, and what language is forbidden in proposals, websites and verbal answers?
How do we sell to a buyer who cannot decide freely - an owner mid-incident, a non-technical sole proprietor, or someone facing an insurer deadline?
In a small business, who actually decides, who pays, who must enforce the controls day to day, and who has the authority to authorize work on each system?
How do we turn a discovery conversation into an exposure picture and a loss band without inventing industry breach-cost numbers?
Which prospects should we decline, and how is a decline delivered without damaging the practice's name in a small market?
What may a free or pre-sales security review actually include, and where does it become unauthorized testing?
How are tiers built so that every control in a package is justified, and why can the cheapest tier never drop below the floor?
What does one seat or one site actually cost us to serve each month, and where does each component of that cost come from?
Which unit do we bill on, how is a seat counted and trued up, and how do vendor price changes reach the client's invoice?
How is the initial hardening project scoped and priced, and what may be discounted when a buyer pushes back on price?
How do we use an insurance questionnaire or a compliance framework as a demand wedge without attesting, auditing, or giving advice we are not qualified to give?
What must the signed proposal contain, what must the client agree to do themselves, and what conditions must be met before deployment is allowed to start?
What has to exist in writing before we touch a single client system, and who has to sign it?

A client asks us to check whether their former bookkeeper can still get into the system, or to test a supplier's portal - what do we do, and where is the line around phishing simulations of their own staff?
How do we build an asset and identity picture we can bill from and defend against, and what happens to the devices and accounts nobody told us about?
How do we tell a client which security obligations may apply to their data without acting as their auditor or their lawyer?
How do we decide what this client's target baseline actually is, given what they already have?
How do we choose the products behind the stack so they stay manageable across many small clients and do not trap us?
In what order should the controls land so the client gets the most risk reduction per unit of disruption?
How do we land a disruptive hardening change without breaking the client's line-of-business software, and what is our way back if we do?
What does deployed actually mean for endpoint protection and patching - how do we prove coverage instead of assuming it?
How do we build backup so an attacker with administrative credentials cannot delete it, and what proves at handover that recovery actually works?
How do we roll out a second factor, mail authentication and edge cleanup without locking the owner out or silently dropping the client's mail?
What do we do with the machine that cannot be patched or the application that demands permanent administrator rights, and how do we describe what the client is still exposed to?
How do we secure our own access into client systems so the practice is not the biggest risk its clients carry?
What proves the hardening project is finished, what do we hand over, and what has to be true before the monthly service starts?
What is the practice actually allowed to do on this client's live systems without stopping to ask, what always needs a named human's approval, and what will it refuse outright?
What does the word monitored mean in this subscription - who is looking, in which hours, and what actually happens to a high-severity alert at three in the morning?
How does the practice describe what its service is doing without claiming protection it cannot deliver and without inflating threat counts to justify the invoice?
Are we actually seeing the whole estate, and how do we catch drift such as a dead agent, a device nobody told us about, or a departed employee whose account still signs in?
How is a generic alert stream tuned to this specific small business without quietly switching off detections that matter?
How do we know whether the alert queue is profitable at the price we charge, and what do we do when one noisy client eats the margin of several quiet ones?
When does an alert become a declared incident, who is allowed to declare it, and what are the first moves for the incidents that actually happen to small businesses?
How do we decide whether to isolate a system the business needs in order to trade, and how do we avoid destroying the evidence while we stop the bleeding?
What exactly do we tell the client during a live incident, on what channel, how often, and what do we say when our own missed alert or unpatched system was part of the path?
When is an incident beyond our competence or authority, who else has to be brought in, and how do we handle notification duties without practising law?
How do we prove this client can actually be restored, how long it really takes, and what will never come back at all?
After an incident, what stops it happening again, and how are the fixes split between what we already owe under the subscription and what is genuinely new scope?
How do we help a client answer an insurer questionnaire, a customer's vendor-security review or a framework control list without becoming their auditor or their lawyer?
Why does a client renew after a year in which nothing visibly happened, and how do we grow the account from what we observed rather than from what we could make them afraid of?
